explain.anyChar: Matches any single character (line breaks only with the s flag).
explain.notDigit: Matches any character that is not a digit.
explain.word: Matches a word character (letter, digit or underscore).
explain.notWord: Matches any character that is not a word character.
explain.space: Matches a whitespace character (space, tab, line break).
explain.wordBoundary: Word boundary: the position between a word character and a non-word character.
explain.backref: Backreference: matches the same text as capture group {{n}}.
explain.namedBackref: Backreference: matches the same text as the group named "{{name}}".
explain.unicodeProp: Matches a character with the Unicode property {{prop}} (needs the u or v flag).
explain.notUnicodeProp: Matches a character WITHOUT the Unicode property {{prop}} (needs the u or v flag).
explain.hexEscape: Matches the character with hex code {{code}}.
explain.class: Matches one character from the set: {{set}}
explain.classNegated: Matches one character NOT in the set: {{set}}
explain.groupCapture: Start of a capturing group (its text is saved).
explain.groupNamed: Start of a capturing group named "{{name}}".
explain.groupNonCapture: Start of a non-capturing group (groups without saving).
explain.lookahead: Positive lookahead: what follows must match, but is not consumed.
explain.negLookahead: Negative lookahead: what follows must NOT match.
explain.lookbehind: Positive lookbehind: what precedes must match.
explain.negLookbehind: Negative lookbehind: what precedes must NOT match.
explain.alternation: OR: matches the expression on the left or on the right.
explain.lineStart: Start of the text (start of each line with the m flag).
explain.lineEnd: End of the text (end of each line with the m flag).
explain.quantStar: Repeats the previous item zero or more times (greedy).
explain.quantPlus: Repeats the previous item one or more times (greedy).
explain.quantOptional: Makes the previous item optional (zero or one time).
explain.quantExact: Repeats the previous item exactly {{n}} times.
explain.quantMin: Repeats the previous item {{n}} or more times.
explain.quantRange: Repeats the previous item between {{min}} and {{max}} times.
explain.quantStarLazy: Repeats the previous item zero or more times, as few as possible (lazy).
explain.quantPlusLazy: Repeats the previous item one or more times, as few as possible (lazy).
explain.quantOptionalLazy: Optional (zero or one time), preferring zero (lazy).
explain.quantExactLazy: Repeats the previous item exactly {{n}} times.
explain.quantMinLazy: Repeats the previous item {{n}} or more times, as few as possible (lazy).
explain.quantRangeLazy: Repeats the previous item between {{min}} and {{max}} times, as few as possible (lazy).

faq.heading: Frequently asked questions
faq.q1: Will a bad regex pattern freeze the page?
faq.a1: No — matching runs in a separate Web Worker with a hard timeout, so even a catastrophic-backtracking pattern can't lock up your tab.
faq.q2: Does it show named and numbered capture groups?
faq.a2: Yes — every match lists its numbered groups and any named groups like (?<year>\d{4}).
faq.q3: Can I preview a replacement before using it in code?
faq.a3: Yes — the Replace panel shows exactly what String.replace() would output, including group backreferences.

article.heading: How does testing a regex in the browser actually work?
article.p1: A regular expression is a compact pattern language for matching text — everything from "does this look like an email address" to "find every phone number in this document" to "strip HTML tags from this string." The catch is that regex syntax is notoriously easy to get subtly wrong: a `.` that should be escaped, a greedy `*` that swallows more than intended, a group that isn't capturing what you expect. Writing one blind and only finding out it's wrong once it's already running against production data is a bad way to learn that lesson.
article.p2: This tool runs entirely on JavaScript's own built-in `RegExp` engine, executing directly in your browser the moment you type — there's no server involved, so whatever text you're testing against (which might be real user data, log lines, or anything else you'd rather not paste into a third-party service) never leaves your machine. Because it's the exact same engine your JavaScript code will run in production, what you see here — which characters match, how greedy quantifiers behave, whether a group captured anything — is exactly what you'll get at runtime, not an approximation from a different regex flavor.
article.p3: Type a pattern and flip on the flags you need: `g` to find every match instead of stopping at the first one, `i` for case-insensitive matching, `m` to make `^` and `$` match the start/end of each line rather than the whole string, `s` to let `.` match newlines too. Every match in your test string is highlighted live, and each one is broken down below into its full matched text, its position, and any capture groups — including named groups like `(?<year>\d{4})` — so you can immediately see whether the group you meant to extract is actually the one that matched. The Replace section shows exactly what `String.replace()` would produce with your pattern and a replacement string, including group backreferences like `$1` or `$<year>`.
article.p4: The quick-reference panel below covers the tokens people forget most often mid-task — the difference between `*` and `+`, what a non-capturing group `(?:...)` is for, how `\b` marks a word boundary — without needing to leave the page to look them up. Once you've got a pattern that behaves the way you want against realistic test data, it's ready to drop straight into your code. If you need to validate or reformat the surrounding data itself, the JSON Formatter & Validator and Text Diff Checker tools are natural companions.
